To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
firm size and employee empowerment are important factors that affect the relationship between absorptive capacity potential and realised absorption of new knowledge.
the negative effect of firm size on the relationship between the potential and realized absorptive capacity can be reduced by increasing employee empowerment.

(a) firm size negatively moderates the relationship between potential absorptive capacity and realised absorptive capability and that (b) employee empowerment positively moderates the negative impact of firm size.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of why some firms are more successful than others in exploiting the knowledge created by others, and why some firms are better at exploiting their own knowledge.
the question of how absorptive capacity is affected by the size of the firm and the degree of empowerment of employees.
the question of how absorptive capacity is affected by the size of a firm.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relationship between a firm's size and its absorptive capacity is contingent upon the degree of employee empowerment.
a large firm can increase its absorptive capacity by empowering employees.
the size of the firm has a negative effect on the relationship between the potential and realised absorption capacity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the absorptive capacity is not an unidimensional construct and its realisation is not a straightforward process.
a larger organisation can be more effective in knowledge creation and exploitation by empowering its employees.
the absorptive capacity literature needs to be extended to include contextual factors, such as firm size, that might affect this relationship and thus the ability to create and apply new knowledge.
The main takeaway from our work is that
large firms can improve their absorptive capacity by empowering their employees.
managers should be careful when implementing knowledge management strategies, especially in large organisations.
the size of a firm can be a double-edged sword.
